analysis.one_liner: Caps what families pay for phone calls to relatives in prison and ends carrier kickbacks to prisons.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House committee it was assigned to, with no vote or hearing recorded in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the FCC to cap the per-minute and per-call rates that phone companies charge for calls made by people in prison. Because inmates can generally only make outgoing calls, their families pay these charges, and the bill's own findings note some rates hit $1 per minute plus a $3.95 connection fee [S3]. It also would have banned the commissions phone carriers pay prisons for the exclusive right to provide service, and required facilities to allow more than one carrier so inmates had a choice [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Families and friends of incarcerated people, who typically pay for prison phone calls, gain the most if rates are capped and commissions that inflate prices are banned. Low-income households benefit disproportionately, since the bill's findings state that families of prisoners are often low-income and bear the cost of some of the highest phone rates in the country [S3]. Incarcerated people also benefit indirectly, as the bill cites research linking regular family contact to lower recidivism and easier reentry [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families paying for calls from prison

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to consider maximum uniform per-minute and per-call rate caps for interstate prison phone calls [S2] [S3].
Prohibits phone carriers from paying commissions to prison administrators for exclusive service contracts, which the bill says can account for 50% or more of total charges [S3].
Requires providers to offer both collect calling and prepaid debit account options, and requires prisons to allow more than one carrier so inmates and families have a choice [S2] [S3].
States that maintaining family contact reduces recidivism and supports rehabilitation, making the rate caps a public safety measure as well as a consumer one [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Inmate telephone service carriers lose revenue from capped rates and banned commissions, and correctional agencies lose the commissions they collect from those carriers, which the bill notes can fund services at facilities. Phone companies with exclusive prison contracts lose their protected market position.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone carriers and corrections agencies

drawbacks.text: Corrections departments relied on commission revenue from phone contracts, and losing it could leave facilities without funding for programs or infrastructure those contracts paid for, a cost that could fall back on state budgets [S3].

Rate caps could reduce carrier incentives to invest in phone systems at prisons, and facilities argue restrictions on calling must not compromise security monitoring, which the bill acknowledges by excluding legitimate penological interests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits fall on low-income families facing some of the highest per-minute rates in the country, with commission payments inflating prices by up to half the total charge. The costs fall on phone carriers and corrections agencies that collect commissions. The bill is a straightforward consumer rate regulation with a clear benefit-cost case, though it delegates the hard work of setting actual rate levels to FCC rulemaking rather than fixing numbers in statute.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Telecommunications Subcommittee and never advanced further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on January 18, 2007, with six original cosponsors including Reps. Boucher, Gutierrez, Wynn, Towns, Cleaver, and Cummings [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and it went to the Telecommunications and the Internet Subcommittee on February 2, 2007 [S5].
No further action, vote, or hearing appears in the record for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009 [S5].
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never advanced past subcommittee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prison phone carriers kept their exclusive contracts and commission payments to prisons, and correctional agencies kept collecting those commissions. Families paying high per-minute rates for calls from prisons gained nothing; the rate caps the bill proposed were never tested in a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone carriers and corrections agencies

industries.note: These carriers held exclusive contracts at correctional facilities and charged among the highest per-minute rates in the country, with commissions to prisons inflating prices further. Rate caps and a ban on commissions would cut their revenue directly.
These agencies collected commissions from phone carriers based on inmate call revenue, in some cases half of total charges. The bill would end that revenue stream.
